vo: Normandy, nineteen forty-four. This American soldier is about to cross one field. He carries a rifle, a shovel, and one day of food.
visual: empty board -> date '1944' writes on top-left, red underline -> soldier stick figure draws on center (olive scribble fill) -> rifle + shovel + ration box pop beside him with labels

vo: But he is not alone. Behind him stands a line of people no war movie shows. How long is that line? By the end, you'll know the exact number.
visual: camera slides left: grey silhouettes draw on behind him one by one, the line runs off-screen -> big red '?' pops at the end of the line

vo: Let's start with something simple. Breakfast. At the front, our soldier often eats a K ration. A small waxed cardboard box of food.
visual: title 'Quest 1: Breakfast' top-left, red underline -> K ration box draws on center, scribble-fill khaki -> label 'K RATION'

vo: Three boxes make one day. Breakfast, dinner, and supper. Together, they hold about two thousand eight hundred and thirty calories.
visual: three boxes slide in a row labelled BREAKFAST / DINNER / SUPPER -> yellow burst around '= 2,830 kcal ='
verify: K ration day = 2,830 kcal

vo: Each box was planned down to small details. Besides the food, there were a few cigarettes, chewing gum, and toilet paper. Somebody, in an office far away, decided all of that.
visual: box lid opens -> small items pop out one by one with labels: cigarettes, gum, toilet paper -> office desk doodle with a clipboard on the right
verify: K ration contents incl. cigarettes, gum, toilet paper — exact items varied by meal unit and year

vo: That sounds like plenty. But it isn't. A man who digs holes and carries ammunition all day burns far more. So front-line soldiers were hungry almost all the time.
visual: soldier digging animation (shovel loop) -> thermometer-style 'energy' bar drains from green to red -> red arrow '<- not enough'

vo: Now ask a strange question. Who made this box? Not an army cook. A factory, thousands of miles away, back in the United States.
visual: board wipe -> world map (Atlantic) draws on -> dotted line from USA to France, label 'thousands of miles' -> factory icon draws on in USA

vo: Farmers grew the food. Factory workers packed it. Railroad crews hauled it to a port. Dockworkers lifted it onto a ship.
visual: four small figures pop in a chain across the USA: farmer -> factory worker -> train -> dockworker, each with a tiny icon (wheat, box, rail, crane)

vo: So before our soldier takes one bite, dozens of people have already touched his breakfast. But food is the easy part. Food does not explode. And food does not sink.
visual: counter '0 -> dozens' above the chain -> ship draws on at the US coast -> red text 'the hard part?'

vo: Everything this soldier uses has to cross the Atlantic Ocean. That is more than three thousand miles of open water.
visual: title 'Quest 2: The Ocean' top-left -> cargo ship moves along the dotted line across the Atlantic -> label '3,000+ miles'
verify: 'more than three thousand miles' New York–UK/France crossing

vo: But German submarines, the U-boats, were hunting the ships that carried it. Every ship that went down took bullets, food, and sometimes men with it.
visual: submarine (steel grey, 'GERMANY' label, no symbols) draws on under the waves -> dashed torpedo line -> one cargo ship icon sinks and fades to an outline, red X on map

vo: So America needed ships. Not a few. Thousands. The answer was the Liberty ship. A simple, slow cargo ship, built almost like a car on an assembly line.
visual: board wipe -> Liberty ship side view draws on in sections (hull, deck, bridge), each section scribble-fills steel grey -> label 'LIBERTY SHIP'
sfx: shipyard rivet hammering (NEW) | marker squeak long (lib)

vo: Many of the welders in those shipyards had never held a torch before the war. Plenty of them were women. They learned in weeks a job that used to take years.
visual: welder figure (woman, headscarf) with torch, yellow spark bursts on the hull -> label 'learned in weeks'
verify: women welders in Liberty yards; 'learned in weeks' = general claim about short training courses

vo: American shipyards built two thousand seven hundred and ten of them. One of them, the Robert E. Peary, went from keel to launch in four days and fifteen hours.
visual: rows of tiny ships multiply to fill the right side -> big number '2,710' with yellow burst -> calendar flips 4 pages + clock '15 h'
verify: 2,710 Liberty ships; Robert E. Peary keel-to-launch 4 days 15 h (sources: 15h29m / 15h30m)

vo: But a ship needs a crew. The men who sailed these cargo ships were mostly civilian merchant mariners. Not soldiers. Yet their job was one of the deadliest at sea.
visual: sailor figure in a knit cap on the deck -> label 'MERCHANT MARINE — civilians' -> small crosses on the Atlantic map behind him (no gore)
verify: US merchant marine casualty rate — often cited ~1 in 26 died, the highest of any US service; we only say 'one of the deadliest'

vo: A ship, in less than a week. That sounds like the problem is solved. But a ship only gets you to the coast. And by the end of summer, our soldier was nowhere near the coast.
visual: ship arrives at Normandy coast on map -> camera pans east across France to the soldier figure far inland -> red arrow between them labelled '?'

vo: By late August nineteen forty-four, the Allied armies had raced across France. The front was hundreds of miles from the beaches. And the French railways had been wrecked by bombing.
visual: title 'Quest 3: The Last Miles' -> Europe map: blue Allied arrows sweep from Normandy toward Paris and beyond -> rail lines draw on and get red X marks
verify: French rail network heavily damaged by Allied pre-invasion bombing

vo: So the Army did something simple. It used trucks. Thousands of trucks, driving day and night on one-way roads closed to everyone else. They called it the Red Ball Express.
visual: one-way loop road draws on the map (red line out, blue line back) -> a truck draws on, then copies itself into a convoy -> red ball icon + label 'RED BALL EXPRESS'
verify: Red Ball Express: one-way loop routes closed to civilian traffic, ran 25 Aug–16 Nov 1944

vo: Most of those trucks were the two-and-a-half-ton workhorse the soldiers called the deuce and a half. Each one was loaded far beyond what it was built for.
visual: close-up: deuce-and-a-half truck draws on, olive scribble-fill -> cargo stack grows taller than the truck -> red arrow '<- overloaded'
verify: GMC CCKW 2.5-ton 'deuce and a half' was the main Red Ball truck; overloading (often double load) is widely reported

vo: On August twenty-ninth, nineteen forty-four, the Red Ball set its record. Five thousand nine hundred and fifty-eight vehicles carried over twelve thousand tons forward. In a single day.
visual: calendar 'AUG 29, 1944' -> counter rolls to '5,958 trucks' -> second counter '12,342 tons' with yellow burst
verify: 29 Aug 1944: 132 truck companies, 5,958 vehicles, 12,342 tons

vo: About three out of four of those drivers were Black soldiers. They served in a segregated army. They drove for days with very little sleep.
visual: close-up: driver stick figure in truck cab, hands on wheel -> label '3 out of 4 drivers' -> clock spins fast behind the cab
verify: ~75% of Red Ball drivers were African American

vo: Some drivers fell asleep at the wheel. Trucks broke down by the thousands. But the convoys kept rolling, because the front was screaming for one thing above all.
visual: truck with cartoon smoke puff + wrench icon -> convoy keeps moving -> big jerrycan draws on center, scribble-fill olive

vo: There was a cruel twist. The longer the road got, the more gasoline the trucks themselves burned. A big share of the fuel was used up just delivering fuel.
visual: jerrycan on a truck, a second gauge on the truck itself drains as it drives -> red arrow loop 'fuel to deliver fuel'
sfx: truck convoy rumble (NEW, reuse) | counter roll (lib)
verify: trucks consumed a large share of fuel carried as routes lengthened — no exact % used in VO

vo: Gasoline. And even this was not enough. At the end of August, General Patton's tanks ground to a halt near the Meuse river. Not because of the Germans. Because the fuel ran out.
visual: tank draws on the map at the Meuse -> fuel gauge needle drops to E -> tank stops, red text 'OUT OF FUEL'
verify: 31 Aug 1944: Third Army crossed the Meuse at Verdun and Commercy; tanks ran dry (of 17 tanks sent to Verdun only 3 arrived) — CMH Lorraine Campaign ch. 1–3; Third Army received ~32,000 gal on 30 Aug, <1/10 of need

vo: So here is our first big clue. Fighting a war is not mostly fighting. It is moving things. And moving things takes people. Lots of people.
visual: board wipe -> handwritten line 'War = moving things' with red underline -> small figures start filling the line behind the soldier from the hook

vo: But soldiers do not run on gasoline. They run on hope. And at the front, hope usually arrived in an envelope.
visual: title 'Quest 4: Mail Call' -> envelope draws on center, heart doodle on the seal -> soldier figure reads, small smile

vo: Millions of letters crossed the ocean. But paper is heavy. Every sack of mail on a ship was space that could have carried shells or food.
visual: stack of mail sacks grows on a ship deck -> balance scale: mail sacks vs. ammo crates, scale tips

vo: So the Army got clever. Letters were photographed onto tiny rolls of film. They called it Victory Mail, or V mail.
visual: letter slides under a camera icon -> shrinks into a film strip -> label 'V-MAIL' hand-lettered, red underline

vo: Thirty-seven mail bags of ordinary letters shrank into one single bag of film. On the other side of the ocean, the film was printed back onto paper and delivered.
visual: 37 small sack icons in a grid -> they collapse into ONE sack, yellow burst '37 -> 1' -> film strip unrolls into a letter on the right
verify: V-mail: 37 bags (150,000 one-page letters) -> 1 sack of film

vo: For a nineteen-year-old in a muddy hole, that letter could be the only proof the world back home still existed. Mothers wrote about the weather. Sisters wrote about weddings. Nobody wrote about the war.
visual: soldier in foxhole holds letter -> thought bubble draws on: a house, a wedding cake, a sun doodle -> war sounds dim

vo: Which means that somewhere behind the front, soldiers spent their whole war printing, sorting, and delivering letters to strangers. Nobody makes movies about them. But every man at the front waited for their work.
visual: three clerk figures at a sorting table, letters flying into pigeonholes -> one letter flies off-screen toward the soldier

vo: Now the hardest moment of the day. Our soldier is wounded. Not badly, but he cannot walk. What happens next?
visual: title 'Quest 5: The Chain' -> soldier figure sits down, small red cross bandage icon on leg (no blood) -> question mark

vo: First, a medic reaches him. He has no hospital. Just a canvas bag and his own two hands. His job is simple and brutal. Buy time.
visual: medic figure with red cross armband draws on, kneels -> canvas bag icon -> clock icon labelled 'buy time'

vo: Litter bearers carry him back. A battalion aid station checks him. An ambulance drives him to a field hospital, where surgeons go to work.
visual: horizontal chain builds left to right: stretcher team -> aid station tent -> ambulance (red cross) -> field hospital tent, connected with arrows

vo: Speed mattered more than anything. A wounded man who reached a surgeon quickly had a far better chance of living. So the whole chain was built to save minutes.
visual: clock with a red sweep hand over the chain -> arrows between stations get shorter -> label 'every minute counts'

vo: Some wounded men went even further. Back to England. Some all the way home. Every step of that trip is handled by a different group of people.
visual: chain extends onto the map: hospital ship to England -> plane icon across the Atlantic -> home icon in the USA

vo: So let's count who we have met. Farmers. Factory workers. Shipbuilders. Sailors. Truck drivers. Mail clerks. Medics. Surgeons. How many of them stand behind one soldier?
visual: board wipe -> back to the hook line: each job appears as a labelled figure in the line behind the soldier, one per word -> red '?' at the end

vo: To answer that, the Army used a strange word. A slice. Not of bread. A division slice.
visual: title 'Quest 6: The Slice' -> loaf of bread doodle draws on, gets a red X -> text 'DIVISION SLICE' writes on

vo: A division is a big army unit. In nineteen forty-four, an American infantry division had a little over fourteen thousand men on paper.
visual: block of 14 small soldier icons (each = 1,000) arranged in a rectangle -> label '1 division = ~14,000 men'
verify: 1944 infantry division TO&E = 14,253

vo: But planners noticed something. Every division in the line needed many more men behind it, in the same theater of war. Just to keep it moving.
visual: around the division block, faded outlines of more blocks start to draw on (trucks, depots, hospitals icons on them)

vo: The division, plus its share of everyone supporting it, is the division slice. And the slice was much bigger than the division itself. How much bigger? Hold that thought.
visual: a pie-shaped wedge (the 'slice') draws around the division + support blocks -> big red '?' on the wedge

vo: Because first, the Army hit a problem nobody expected. By late nineteen forty-four, America had the biggest army in its history. Around eight million people in the Army alone.
visual: title 'Quest 7: The Shortage' -> big counter rolls up to '~8,000,000' with yellow burst -> crowd of tiny icons fills the board

vo: But in Europe, generals were running out of one kind of soldier. Not drivers. Not cooks. Not clerks. Riflemen.
visual: icons 'driver', 'cook', 'clerk' each get a green check -> rifleman icon gets a red empty box -> red underline under 'RIFLEMEN'

vo: Rifle companies were losing men faster than new ones could arrive. Over months of fighting, some infantry divisions lost more men in total than they had on the first day.
visual: bar chart: division strength 14,000 vs. total losses bar growing past it, empty helmets as bar markers (no gore)
verify: some ETO infantry divisions had >100% battle casualties vs. authorised strength (e.g. 4th, 9th, 29th, 90th ID)

vo: So the Army pulled men from other jobs. Anti-aircraft gunners, clerks, and air force trainees were sent to infantry training and handed rifles.
visual: figures with job icons (AA gun, typewriter, plane) walk through a door labelled 'INFANTRY' and come out with rifles
verify: AAF trainees / ASTP / anti-aircraft and service troops retrained as infantry replacements, late 1944–early 1945

vo: In late December nineteen forty-four, the Army even asked Black service troops to volunteer for combat. Thousands stepped forward. Many sergeants gave up their stripes, just for the chance to fight.
visual: calendar 'DEC 1944' -> figures step forward one by one -> sergeant stripes peel off a sleeve -> label 'volunteers'
verify: Lee's call for Black volunteers 26 Dec 1944; NCOs had to accept reduction to private

vo: About two thousand two hundred of them went to the front in thirty-seven platoons. So here is the real question. How can an army of eight million run out of riflemen?
visual: 37 small platoon icons draw on in a grid -> pull back: tiny rifleman group vs. huge '8,000,000' crowd -> red '?'
verify: ~2,253 volunteers in 37 platoons (first group), assigned to divisions in March 1945

vo: Let's do the math. Our soldier is in a rifle company. A rifle company had about one hundred and ninety-three men. An infantry division had twenty-seven of them.
visual: title 'The Answer' top-left, red double underline -> company icon '193' x 27 grid draws on
verify: rifle company = 193 men (TO&E 15 Jul 1943 / 1944); 27 rifle companies per infantry division

vo: Twenty-seven times one hundred and ninety-three is about five thousand two hundred men. Out of fourteen thousand. So even inside a division, most men were not in rifle companies.
visual: handwritten math '27 x 193 = 5,211' -> division block: 5,200 highlighted red, the rest grey -> label 'riflemen companies'

vo: Now zoom out to Europe. In June nineteen forty-five, each American division there came with a slice of about thirty-five thousand five hundred men.
visual: camera zooms out: division block sits inside a much bigger slice wedge -> counter '35,480' with yellow burst -> date 'JUNE 1945'
verify: ETO division slice 30 June 1945 = 35,480 (Coakley & Leighton, Global Logistics and Strategy 1943–1945, p. 840)

vo: Divide the slice by the men in rifle companies. The answer is almost seven. Almost seven Americans in Europe for every one man in a rifle company.
visual: handwritten '35,480 / 5,211 = 6.8' -> big '1 : 7' with yellow burst -> one red soldier, six grey figures behind him

vo: Six other men in the theater for every rifleman. Drivers, engineers, gunners, mechanics, cooks, clerks, medics. All of them needed, all of them working. But only one of them walks across the field.
visual: the six grey figures each get a job icon (truck, wrench, cannon, pot, typewriter, red cross) -> only the red soldier steps forward

vo: But we are not done. Add the air force, the training camps, and everyone in uniform back home. Divide the whole Army by its eighty-nine divisions. That is over ninety thousand men each.
visual: zoom out again: Europe slice shrinks into a world map, USA fills with figures -> math '8,270,000 / 89 = ~93,000'
verify: 8,267,958 Army (incl. AAF) / 89 divisions ≈ 92,900; Wikipedia cites worldwide slice ≈ 90,200

vo: Divide that by the men in rifle companies. About eighteen. For every soldier walking toward the enemy, seventeen others in uniform stood behind him. And that is before we count a single farmer or factory worker.
visual: final reveal: '1 : 18' huge, yellow burst, red underline -> the hook line completes: 1 red soldier + 17 grey figures, then factory/farm icons fade in behind them
verify: derived: ~92,900 / 5,211 ≈ 17.8 → 'about eighteen' (our own calculation)

vo: This was not waste. It is why the American soldier usually had food, ammunition, and letters from home. But the system had a price.
visual: check marks pop next to ration box, ammo crate, envelope -> scale tips, red text 'the price'

vo: Infantrymen were only a small part of the Army. Yet of every four Army soldiers killed in ground combat, about three were infantrymen. A tiny tip on a giant spear, taking almost every hit.
visual: left: Army crowd block with a small red infantry slice -> right: 4 empty-helmet icons, 3 of them turn red, label '3 of 4' (no gore) -> spear doodle with a red tip
sfx: marker squeak short (lib) | distant artillery boom (lib)
verify: 142,962 of 191,701 Army ground battle deaths were infantrymen ≈ 75% (MWI West Point, citing Army casualty data)

vo: So the next time you watch a war movie, remember the line behind the soldier. Seventeen people working so one man could cross that field. And one man, carrying the war for all of them.
visual: return to the opening field: the soldier stands at the hedge, the long line of figures behind him slowly fades to warm white -> soldier remains

vo: Germany built its army very differently. It invaded the Soviet Union with hundreds of thousands of horses. Why? That is the next video. Subscribe so you don't miss it.
visual: board wipe -> horse doodle draws on next to a tank with a 'GERMANY' label (Balkenkreuz only) -> red '?' -> end card space
verify: German army invaded USSR with roughly 600,000–750,000 horses
